docs.title: How to use claude-cowork-code
docs.text: This is the team handbook for the Cowork + Claude Code way of building software at TAP. It assumes nothing about Frappe — the method works on any stack. Where TAP LMS is used as an example, it's labelled.

docs.title: What this gives you
docs.text:
• Cowork does the thinking on paper — ideas, specs, change requests, reviews.
  • Claude Code does the building — code, tests, running things, maintaining the agent layer.
  • A set of subagents that each own one step (write the PRD, scope the change, build it, review it, test it), and a memory + retrospective loop that turns recurring mistakes into rules so the project gets more correct over time.

The whole thing is held together by one rule: two tools, one folder, never the same file at once. Handoffs go through named files, not chat.

docs.title: Pick your path
docs.text: You are… Read New to the system, setting it up Getting started Standing this up on a new project / microservice Adopt it for a new project In product — have an idea or a bug to report Product playbook In engineering — building or changing a feature Engineering playbook Wanting to understand why it's built this way Methodology Publishing these docs Publishing

docs.title: Reading order (first time)
docs.text:
1. Getting started — install the two tools, open a project, confirm it's wired.
  2. Methodology — the mental model: the two-tool rule, the agents, the memory loop. ~10 min.
  3. Then whichever playbook matches your role (product or engineering).
  4. When you start a new repo: Adopt it for a new project.

docs.title: The shape of a day
docs.text:
Cowork:  "Write a PRD for X"           → docs/prds/PRD-NNN.md
Cowork:  "Write a CR for behavior Y"   → docs/change-requests/CR-NNN.md
  (you review and approve the doc)
Code:    "Implement CR-NNN"            → code + tests, then review + test run
  (you copy to the running env, commit, deploy)
Code:    "Run retrospective"           → the system learns from the work

Same loop on every project. The agents and skills change per stack; the loop doesn't.

docs.title: Adopt it for a new project
docs.text: You're starting a new TAP feature in its own repo, or a brand-new microservice (FastAPI, Node, a data pipeline). This page shows how to stand up the Cowork + Claude Code system there.

docs.title: The model: bootstrap fresh, don't fork
docs.text:
Do not copy claude-cowork-code into your new repo. Most of what's here is TAP-LMS-specific — the frappe-* skills, the Frappe/Postgres rules baked into feature-builder / code-reviewer / test-runner, the accumulated lessons. Dragging those into a FastAPI service is pure noise.

Instead, run four bootstrap prompts in your new repo. They make Claude Code discover your stack and generate an agent layer that fits it. The methodology comes over; the Frappe baggage doesn't. The prompts live in docs/cowork-bootstrap.md — copy them from there; this page is the orientation around them.

Why discovery beats a template: a template bakes in assumptions (build command, test runner, language). Discovery asks. That's what makes the same four prompts work for a Frappe app, a FastAPI service, and a Node API without edits.

docs.title: Before you start — three decisions
docs.text:
Prompt 0 will ask you these. Decide in advance:

Decision Recommended default Why Where is the agent layer tracked? Inside the new code repo Simplest. Use a separate repo only if the code repo must stay deployable/clean. Self-improvement autonomy Proposal-only for ~the first month The retrospective suggests memory/agent edits; you apply the good ones. Graduate to closed-loop once proposals are consistently good. Which agents The full 8 only if the project warrants it A small service can start with feature-builder + code-reviewer + test-runner + retrospective and add prd-author / change-requirement / architecture-reviewer / task-manager when the planning load shows up.

docs.title: The four prompts
docs.text:
Open Claude Code in the new repo and paste them in order, waiting for each to finish.

# Prompt What it does Writes anything? 0 Discovery Inspects stack, build/test commands, git root, any existing .claude/, and whether code runs from a separate location (symlink needed?). Then proposes a plan and asks the three decisions above. No — read-only 1 Scaffold Creates CLAUDE.md, WORKFLOW.md, .claude/agents/ (each with an ## INVARIANTS (do not edit) fence), and .claude/memory/ (lessons, patterns, circuit-breaker, empty logs). Uses the build/test commands it discovered. Yes — commits the layer 2 Retrospective agent Adds .claude/agents/retrospective.md in proposal-only mode, with its own INVARIANTS (it can never weaken them, even on itself). Yes 3 Seed + verify Drafts initial lessons from your git history (you approve), then dry-runs the retrospective in report-only mode and verifies the whole setup. Proposes, then applies what you confirm

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
After the four prompts your new repo has:

your-service/
├── CLAUDE.md            ← project context: YOUR stack, build/test commands, conventions
├── WORKFLOW.md          ← the path-per-task-type map, same shape as TAP's
├── .claude/
│   ├── agents/          ← agents generated for YOUR stack
│   └── memory/          ← lessons.md, patterns.md, circuit-breaker.json, *.jsonl
└── (your code)

No skills/frappe-*, no TAP lessons — a clean layer that knows your build and test commands.

docs.title: What carries over vs. what gets regenerated
docs.text:
Carries over near-verbatim Regenerated for your stack prd-author — writing PRDs/BRs is stack-agnostic feature-builder — knows your language, framework, test idioms change-requirement — CR scoping is universal code-reviewer — checks your stack's footguns (not Postgres/Frappe) architecture-reviewer — the COMPATIBLE / MINOR / ADR verdict model test-runner — runs your test command task-manager — decomposition is universal skills/ — written for your stack (e.g. fastapi-*, pytest) instead of frappe-* retrospective — the learning loop itself .claude/memory/ — your project's lessons, seeded from your history The two-tool rule + file-handoff discipline CLAUDE.md — your conventions

The roles are the reusable asset. Their bodies are stack-specific and the bootstrap writes them fresh.

docs.title: Worked example — a FastAPI microservice
docs.text:
You're building tap-notifications, a FastAPI service. After the four prompts:

  • CLAUDE.md records: Python 3.12, FastAPI, uv/pip, tests = pytest, lint = ruff, the repo layout.
  • skills/ holds something like fastapi-endpoints, pydantic-models, pytest-fixtures, sqlalchemy-migrations — not frappe-*.
  • feature-builder writes endpoints + Pydantic models + pytest tests in the same commit (the "tests in the same commit" rule carries over; the framework doesn't).
  • code-reviewer checks for FastAPI footguns (sync work in async handlers, unvalidated input) instead of Postgres-vs-MariaDB.
  • test-runner runs pytest -q.
  • prd-author, change-requirement, architecture-reviewer, task-manager, retrospective are essentially the TAP versions with the Frappe references swapped out.

The daily loop is identical to TAP's — only the skills and the three build-loop agents differ.

docs.title: A note on memory tiers (MVP)
docs.text: The bootstrap prompts offer a two-tier memory (lessons.md for load-bearing rules + observations.md for high-churn field notes). TAP LMS deliberately started single-tier (lessons.md only) per its MVP discipline and deferred the second tier until volume justified it. Start single-tier. Add observations.md only when lessons.md is genuinely too noisy to scan. Build the minimum; let evidence pull you to more.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Prompt 0 ran read-only and you answered the three decisions.
  • [ ] Prompt 1 created CLAUDE.md, WORKFLOW.md, .claude/agents/ (each with an INVARIANTS fence), .claude/memory/.
  • [ ] Prompt 2 added retrospective in proposal-only mode.
  • [ ] Prompt 3's seeded lessons were reviewed and the dry-run looked sane.
  • [ ] The verify step confirms: build command works, test command runs, all agent files + memory files exist.
  • [ ] You can drive it: "Write a PRD for X", "Implement CR-NNN", "review the last commits", "run retrospective".

Then open the matching playbook — product or engineering — and start shipping.

docs.title: Engineering playbook — CR → build → release
docs.text: For engineers. You live in Claude Code (the build half). You build from named documents, not from chat — a tasks file, a CR, or a BR. This page walks the loop from "there's a spec" to "it's released."

docs.title: What you build from
docs.text:
Inbound Source of truth Start with New feature (from a PRD) docs/.../*-tasks.md (task-manager's output) "Implement TASK-NNN" Behavior change docs/change-requests/CR-NNN-*.md "Implement CR-NNN" Non-trivial bug docs/bug-reports/BR-NNN-*.md (+ tasks) "Implement the BR-NNN fix" Refactor / one-shot tech work a direct task just describe it

The CR gate: if a CR is still Status: Proposed, feature-builder will stop and ask. Never build against a draft — wait for the approver to flip it to Approved (after which the body is immutable).

docs.title: 1. Write the change request (for behavior changes)
docs.text:
If you're changing how an existing feature works, the change starts as a CR, not code:

"Write a CR for: drop students at end of grace instead of pausing."

change-requirement interviews you and writes CR-NNN with the required sections: Motivation, Current Behavior, Proposed Behavior, Scope, Migration, Edge Cases, Acceptance Criteria, Test Plan, Rollback. If it touches schema or system topology, it pulls in architecture-reviewer. The approver flips it to Approved — now it's the build's source of truth.

docs.title: 2. Build it
docs.text:
"Implement CR-NNN" (or "Implement TASK-NNN")

feature-builder reads memory + the CR/PRD + the relevant skills, then builds top-down (data model → logic → API → tests). Two rules it won't break:

  • Tests ship in the same commit as any function with a side effect. No "I'll add tests later."
  • ADR gate: if the work surfaces an un-made architecture decision (new external service, new scheduling cadence, new perf constraint), it stops and spawns architecture-reviewer before continuing.

It ends with a handoff: files changed, acceptance-criteria status, the exact commands to run, and a deploy checklist generated from what the diff touched.

docs.title: 3. Review + test (runs for you)
docs.text:
After a build, the policy is to spawn code-reviewer and test-runner in parallel automatically (trivial edits skip them, and Claude says so). You can also call them by hand:

"Review the diff" · "Run tests"

code-reviewer checks correctness, security, idioms, and that every acceptance criterion has a covering test. test-runner runs the suite and files a task per failure. Recurring findings escalate to the retrospective agent, which turns them into rules so the same mistake doesn't return.

Don't release until review is clean and tests are green.

docs.title: 4. Release
docs.text:
The build loop is automated; release is deliberately manual — a human runs the deploy. The steady-state loop for most services:

review clean + tests green
      ↓
merge / push to the deploy branch
      ↓
run migrations (if any)
      ↓
deploy / restart the service
      ↓
smoke-test the change in the running env
      ↓
watch logs / errors for a short window

Generic release checklist:

  • [ ] Review clean, tests green on the target branch.
  • [ ] Migrations are idempotent and run cleanly on a fresh DB.
  • [ ] Config / secrets / feature flags the change needs are in place.
  • [ ] A rollback path exists (previous build + DB backup) and you know the trigger.
  • [ ] Post-deploy smoke test passes against the running env.
  • [ ] Error/queue volume watched for a window after cutover.

docs.title: TAP LMS release specifics
docs.text:
TAP LMS adds two wrinkles — read these before deploying TAP:

  • Two-folder sync (L-024): you edit app/ in this folder; the bench at ~/frappe-bench/apps/tap_lms is what Frappe runs. Flow: edit here → copy to bench → commit + push from bench → pull back so this folder stays current. Never re-copy files into the bench after the bench has pulled them from git — that creates the untracked-file condition that blocks git pull.
  • The deployment runbook: the full, hard-won procedure (pre-flight probes, bench migrate, bench restart, smoke tests, rollback tree) is docs/deployment-runbook.md. Note it's written for the first-time install; a routine incremental release follows the shorter loop above (copy → commit/push → bench migrate → bench restart → smoke test), using the runbook's smoke-test and rollback sections.
  • migrate vs restart: bench migrate syncs schema + scheduler jobs; bench restart reloads code. Some changes need both — the build handoff's deploy checklist tells you which.

docs.title: 5. Publish the docs (if changed)
docs.text: If the change updates published docs, see Publishing.

docs.title: 6. Close the loop
docs.text:
After a meaningful chunk of work — especially if review caught something — run:

"Run retrospective"

It reads recent reviews, test failures, and git history, and proposes (or, in closed-loop mode, applies) edits to skills/agents/memory so the next build is more correct. This is the part that compounds.

docs.title: Your phrasebook
docs.text:
• "Write a CR for …" — scope a behavior change → change-requirement
  • "Implement CR-NNN" / "Implement TASK-NNN" — build it → feature-builder
  • "Review the diff" / "Review the last N commits" → code-reviewer
  • "Run tests" / "did I break anything" → test-runner
  • "Does our architecture support …" → architecture-reviewer
  • "Run retrospective" — learn from the work → retrospective

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
CR-012: certificate is re-issued every time the completion endpoint is hit (should be once).

  1. "Implement CR-012." feature-builder reads the CR, restates scope, lists files, adds an idempotency guard + a test asserting a second call doesn't re-issue — same commit.
  2. code-reviewer + test-runner run: review clean, tests green.
  3. Release: copy to bench, commit/push, bench migrate (no schema change here, so really just bench restart), smoke-test the endpoint twice, confirm one certificate.
  4. "Run retrospective" — if the bug class (missing idempotency) has recurred, it becomes a rule.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: Goal: get both tools pointed at one project folder and confirm the agent layer is wired. ~15 minutes.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Claude account with Claude Code and Cowork access.
  • git, and clone/read access to the project repo (for TAP work, claude-cowork-code).
  • Node.js (for the Claude Code CLI install method below).
  • For TAP LMS specifically: a working Frappe bench on your machine — see SETUP.md. Not needed if you're only planning, or starting a non-Frappe project.

docs.title: 1. Get the project folder
docs.text:
git clone <your-project-repo>
cd <your-project>

Everything — code, docs, the .claude/ agent layer — lives under this one folder. Both tools open it.

docs.title: 2. Install Claude Code (the build half)
docs.text:
Claude Code is the CLI with a terminal. The common install:

npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code
claude            # run inside the project folder; sign in when prompted

(See the official Claude Code docs for the latest install options, including the native installer and IDE extensions.) On first run in the folder, Claude Code auto-loads CLAUDE.md as context.

docs.title: 3. Open the same folder in Cowork (the plan half)
docs.text:
Cowork is the planning half. Open the same project folder there. Cowork can read and edit files (specs, PRDs, CRs, reviews) but has no terminal and cannot write .claude/. That split is intentional — it's what keeps planning and building from colliding.

Most projects need no "linking" — both tools just open the same folder. The one exception is a framework that runs code from a separate location (e.g. Frappe's bench): there you symlink that location into the folder. The bootstrap discovery prompt (next page) detects this for you.

docs.title: 4. The one rule to internalise
docs.text: Two tools, one folder — never write the same file at the same time. Plan in Cowork → build in Claude Code → review in Cowork. Sequential. Handoffs travel through named files (a PRD, a CR in docs/), never through chat memory. Full reasoning in Methodology.

docs.title: 5. Verify the wiring
docs.text:
In Claude Code, ask:

"List the agents and skills in this project, and tell me when each one fires."

For a TAP LMS checkout it should name eight agents (prd-author, change-requirement, architecture-reviewer, task-manager, feature-builder, code-reviewer, test-runner, retrospective) and eight frappe-* skills. If it can, the layer is loaded correctly.

Then a read-only smoke check:

"Read CLAUDE.md and WORKFLOW.md and summarise the path for a new feature vs. a behavior change."

If the summary matches WORKFLOW.md, you're set.

docs.title: 6. (TAP LMS only) wire the bench
docs.text: TAP LMS runs from a Frappe bench, so app/ is a symlink into ~/frappe-bench/apps/tap_lms. Bench commands run from ~/frappe-bench. Full steps and the two-folder sync rules: SETUP.md.

docs.title: Where to next
docs.text:
• Starting a brand-new repo/microservice → Adopt it for a new project.
  • In product → Product playbook.
  • In engineering → Engineering playbook.
  • Want the mental model first → Methodology.

docs.title: Methodology — why it's built this way
docs.text: The agents and skills change per project. These principles don't. Understanding them is what lets you drive the system instead of just typing at it.

docs.title: The problem this solves
docs.text: An LLM building software on its own tends to: lose context between sessions, repeat mistakes it already made, and blur planning into building until nobody can tell what was decided versus improvised. This system is six principles that fight each of those.

docs.title: 1. Two tools, one folder
docs.text:
Cowork plans. Claude Code builds. They share one folder and never write the same file at the same time.

Planning (specs, CRs, reviews) and building (code, tests) are different modes of thought, and interleaving them is how half-built ideas get shipped. Splitting them across two tools — one without a terminal — makes the boundary physical. Work flows plan → build → review, sequentially.

docs.title: 2. Documents are the interface
docs.text:
Handoffs travel through named files in docs/, never through chat memory:

  • PRD — the what & why of a new feature.
  • BR — a bug report for a non-trivial defect.
  • CR — a scoped change to existing behavior. Immutable once approved — append-only after.
  • ADR — an architecture decision, with its trade-offs, recorded forever.

A document is reviewable, diffable, and survives the session. Chat doesn't. "Implement CR-012" works tomorrow, on another machine, for another person — because CR-012 is a file. This is also what lets the Cowork↔Code boundary exist at all: the tools don't share memory, but they share the folder.

docs.title: 3. One agent per step
docs.text:
Eight narrow roles instead of one do-everything agent. Each does a single job well and hands off:

prd-author → (architecture-reviewer?) → task-manager → feature-builder → code-reviewer + test-runner
change-requirement → (architecture-reviewer?) → feature-builder → code-reviewer + test-runner
                                                                          ↓ (recurring issue)
                                                                    retrospective

Narrow agents are easier to trust, easier to review, and easier to regenerate for a new stack. A wide agent hides its reasoning; a narrow one's output is a checkable artifact.

docs.title: 4. INVARIANTS — constraints that can't be self-edited
docs.text:
Every agent file has a fenced ## INVARIANTS (do not edit) block listing its core job and the rules it must never weaken — even when the system is editing itself. The retrospective agent (principle 5) can rewrite skills and agents, but it is forbidden from touching anything inside an INVARIANTS fence, including its own. To change an invariant, it files a task for a human.

This is the safety rail that makes self-improvement safe: the system can get smarter without being able to remove its own guardrails.

docs.title: 5. Memory that compounds
docs.text:
The system remembers, in .claude/memory/:

  • lessons.md — load-bearing rules. Append-and-supersede only: a rule is never reworded or deleted; a wrong one is marked superseded with a pointer (ADR-style), so the history of why survives.
  • patterns.md — canonical code idioms to reuse instead of reinventing.
  • Append logs — code-review findings, test failures, decisions.

The retrospective agent reads all of it plus recent git history, finds patterns (a mistake that recurs ≥3 times, or one high-consequence bug), and turns each into a one-line rule that prevents the next occurrence. It audits its own past edits, too — a rule that didn't actually reduce the problem it targeted gets flagged.

Two safety dials:

  • Autonomy — start proposal-only (it suggests; you apply). Graduate to closed-loop (it auto-applies, git is the rollback) once proposals are consistently good.
  • Circuit breaker — lanes (skills, agents, memory) that can be paused. A closed lane blocks writes there until a human reopens it.

This is the compounding part: each recurring mistake becomes a rule, so the project gets more correct over time instead of drifting.

docs.title: 6. Build the minimum, prove it, then expand
docs.text: Tooling follows the same MVP discipline as features: build only what the current work needs; expand because a measurement failed or a real need showed up, never because building has momentum. TAP LMS started single-tier memory and deferred a second tier, deferred a weekly cron, and kept deployment manual — each revisited only when evidence demanded. Apply the same restraint to your own layer: don't add an agent, a memory tier, or a skill until the work asks for it.

docs.title: The payoff
docs.text:
Plan and build stop colliding (1, 2). Decisions become durable and reviewable (2). Each step is a checkable artifact (3). The system can improve itself without removing its guardrails (4, 5). And it stays small until evidence says otherwise (6).

The result: a build loop that closes itself — write the spec, build it, review and test it, learn from it — and gets more correct the longer you run it.

→ Now apply it: Product playbook · Engineering playbook · Adopt it for a new project

docs.title: Product playbook — idea → BR / PRD
docs.text: For product folks. You mostly live in Cowork (the planning half). Your job is to turn ideas and problems into the named documents engineering builds from. You don't need to touch code.

docs.title: Pick the right document
docs.text:
Three situations, three entry agents. Getting this right saves a rewrite:

You have… Entry agent Output Say A new capability ("students should get a certificate") prd-author docs/prds/PRD-NNN-*.md "Write a PRD for …" A non-trivial bug ("re-engagement fires after opt-out") prd-author (bug mode) docs/bug-reports/BR-NNN-*.md "Write a bug report for …" A change to how an existing feature works ("drop students at end of grace instead of pausing") change-requirement docs/change-requests/CR-NNN-*.md "Write a CR for …"

Rule of thumb: new thing → PRD. Broken thing → BR. Different thing → CR. prd-author auto-picks PRD vs. BR by scope; you don't have to.

docs.title: The flow
docs.text:
(optional) brainstorm in Cowork
      ↓
"Write a PRD for X"   →  prd-author asks you clarifying questions
      ↓
PRD-NNN lands in docs/prds/   ←  you read it, correct it, approve it
      ↓
"Decompose this into tasks"   →  task-manager → docs/.../*-tasks.md
      ↓
(handoff to engineering — see the Engineering playbook)

docs.title: 1. Brainstorm first (optional but recommended)
docs.text:
Before committing to a doc, think out loud with Claude in Cowork — pressure-test the problem, who it's for, what success looks like, what you're not doing. Cowork ships product brainstorming skills you can lean on. A good brainstorm gives prd-author sharper raw material and means fewer clarifying rounds.

You don't have to brainstorm — if the idea is clear, go straight to "Write a PRD for …".

docs.title: 2. Let prd-author interview you
docs.text: prd-author will probe: the problem, the user, the goal, scope (and non-goals), success metrics, acceptance criteria. Answer plainly. It will also flag if your idea actually raises an architecture question and pull in architecture-reviewer — that's a feature, not a delay; it means a real decision gets recorded as an ADR before code is written.

docs.title: 3. What a good PRD/BR looks like
docs.text:
You're the approver, so know the bar:

  • Problem & why now — the pain, not the solution.
  • User & goal — who, and what they can do after.
  • Scope and non-goals — non-goals are the most valuable lines in the doc; they prevent scope creep.
  • Success metrics — how you'll know it worked.
  • Acceptance criteria — concrete, testable statements. Engineering turns each into a test.
  • (BR) Repro steps + expected vs. actual.

If a section is hand-wavy, send it back before approving. A vague PRD becomes a vague feature.

docs.title: 4. Approve, then hand off
docs.text:
When the PRD reads right, say "Decompose this into tasks" — task-manager breaks it into a backlog and writes a tasks file. That file is the handoff to engineering. (Task lists don't cross the Cowork↔Code boundary; the file does.)

For a behavior change, the gate is different: you flip the CR's Status: Proposed → Approved. After approval the CR body is immutable — further changes are append-only. That immutability is what lets feature-builder trust it as the source of truth.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Idea: "Students should get a certificate when they finish a program."

  1. (Cowork) Brainstorm: who downloads it, what's on it, what about partial completion? Decide certificates are completion-only (non-goal: partial/streak certs, v1).
  2. (Cowork) "Write a PRD for certificate-on-completion." prd-author asks: trigger condition? format (PDF/image)? who can re-download? You answer.
  3. PRD-007 lands in docs/prds/. You read it — the non-goals capture the v1 boundary. You approve.
  4. "Decompose this into tasks." task-manager writes the tasks file: certificate DocType, generation on completion, download endpoint, tests.
  5. Engineering picks it up → Engineering playbook.

docs.title: Your phrasebook
docs.text:
• "Brainstorm a feature for …" — think it through first
  • "Write a PRD for …" — new capability → prd-author
  • "Write a bug report for …" — non-trivial bug → prd-author (BR mode)
  • "Write a CR for …" — change an existing behavior → change-requirement
  • "Does our architecture support …" — sanity-check feasibility → architecture-reviewer
  • "Decompose this into tasks" — ready to hand off → task-manager

docs.title: Publishing the guide
docs.text: How this handbook gets to a public GitHub Pages site while the source repo stays private.

docs.title: The model: private source, public render
docs.text:
claude-cowork-code is a private repo. GitHub Pages can't serve a private site on the current plan, so we don't try. Instead — exactly as the tap-lms-docs site already works — we render the Markdown and push only the built HTML to a separate public repo, whose Pages serves it.

guide/  (private repo)  --mkdocs build-->  HTML  --gh-deploy-->  public docs repo (gh-pages)  -->  Pages URL

Your private source, history, and the rest of the repo never leave the private repo. Only the rendered guide is public.

docs.title: What goes public
docs.text:
This is a separate site from the TAP-LMS product docs (mkdocs.yml → published/). The guide site is configured by mkdocs-guide.yml with docs_dir: guide — so only files under guide/ are published. Nothing else in the repo is rendered.

Keep guide/ generic. It's the public face: no credentials, no internal hostnames, no TAP-LMS internals beyond what's already labelled as examples. The docs_dir: guide boundary is your allowlist — anything you don't want public simply doesn't go in guide/.

docs.title: First-time setup (once)
docs.text:
1. Create a public docs repo. Either in the org (e.g. theapprenticeproject/claude-cowork-code-guide) or a public personal repo. This repo holds only the rendered output.

  2. Add it as a git remote named guide-site: bash git remote add guide-site https://github.com/<owner>/<public-docs-repo>.git

  3. Ensure the docs venv exists (shared with the tap-lms-docs site): bash python3 -m venv .docs-venv .docs-venv/bin/pip install mkdocs-material

  4. Publish: bash ./scripts/publish-guide.sh It builds guide/ with --strict, shows you the target remote, asks for confirmation (the push is public and hard to undo), then gh-deploys to the gh-pages branch of guide-site.

  5. Enable Pages on the public repo: Settings → Pages → Source = gh-pages branch. The URL appears there (e.g. https://<owner>.github.io/<public-docs-repo>/).

  6. Record the URL in README.md and guide/index.md where they say "set after first deploy".

docs.title: Routine publish
docs.text:
After the one-time setup, every update is one command:

./scripts/publish-guide.sh

The gh CLI must be authed as an account with push access to the public repo (here, nithun). Run gh auth status to check.

docs.title: Adding or changing pages
docs.text:
• Drop a new .md into guide/ — it appears in the menu automatically (the config has no nav: block; the menu is built from the files). Add a curated nav: to mkdocs-guide.yml later if you want titles/ordering.
  • Cross-link with relative .md paths ([Methodology](methodology.md)) — mkdocs rewrites them to the right URLs. The same links also work when browsing guide/ directly on GitHub.
  • Re-run ./scripts/publish-guide.sh to push the update.

docs.title: Why two sites, not one
docs.text: The TAP-LMS product docs and this methodology guide have different audiences and different public-vs-internal boundaries. Keeping them as two mkdocs configs (mkdocs.yml and mkdocs-guide.yml) with two site_dirs (site/ and site-guide/) means publishing one never touches the other.
